desc:
A flip at a node swaps its left and right children (together with their whole subtrees); a missing child can be swapped with a real one too. Two binary trees a and b are flip equivalent if a can be turned into a tree identical to b by performing some number of flips, each at any node, possibly none.

Return true if the two given trees are flip equivalent and false otherwise. Two empty trees are flip equivalent. Values may repeat, so you cannot match nodes by value alone.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

Both arguments use this encoding. For a = [1, 2, 3, 4] and b = [1, 3, 2, -1, -1, -1, 4] the answer is true: flip the root of a, then flip node 2 so that its child 4 moves to the right. For a = [1, 2, 3] and b = [1, 2, 4] it is false, because no sequence of flips can change a value.
constraints: 0 ≤ number of nodes in each tree ≤ 1,500
Every tree array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Compare the two roots first. If their values differ, no flips can help. If they match, what are the only two ways their children can be paired up?
Either the left subtree matches the left subtree and right matches right, or the left matches the right and right matches the left. Flips below can be chosen independently in each pair.

With repeated values a naive 'try both pairings' recursion can take exponential time. Give every subtree a canonical id: the key (value, smaller child id, larger child id) looked up in a shared dictionary. Two subtrees are flip equivalent exactly when their ids are equal.
editorial: Flipping a node only reorders its two children, so the set of trees reachable from a tree is determined by treating each node's children as an unordered pair. Two trees are flip equivalent exactly when, recursively, the root values are equal and the two child subtrees of one root can be matched with the two child subtrees of the other root in either order.

The direct recursion f(x, y) = (f(xl, yl) and f(xr, yr)) or (f(xl, yr) and f(xr, yl)) is fine when values are distinct, because then at most one pairing can have matching roots. With repeated values (for example two long chains of zeros, one leaning left and the other zig-zagging) both pairings may be tried at every level and the running time explodes.

The robust solution assigns each subtree a canonical id bottom-up. The id of a node is looked up in one dictionary shared by both trees under the key (value, min(leftId, rightId), max(leftId, rightId)), with id 0 for a missing child. By induction two subtrees get the same id exactly when they are flip equivalent. The answer is whether the two root ids are equal. Every node is processed once: O(n + m) expected time.
